directAnswer: To compress files on a Mac, you can use the built-in 'Compress' feature available in Finder. This allows you to create a ZIP file of selected items quickly.
summary: Compressing files on a Mac is straightforward using Finder's built-in functionality, which allows for easy file management and sharing.

sections.heading: How to Compress Files Using Finder
sections.body: Finder provides a simple way to compress files into a ZIP format. This method is efficient for reducing file sizes and grouping multiple files.

sections.heading: Alternative Compression Tools
sections.body: While Finder is convenient, there are third-party applications available, such as Keka or The Unarchiver, that offer additional compression formats and options.

steps.title: Select Files or Folders
steps.detail: Open Finder and select the files or folders you want to compress. You can hold down the Command key to select multiple items.

steps.title: Compress Selected Items
steps.detail: Right-click on the selected items and choose 'Compress' from the context menu. Alternatively, you can go to the 'File' menu at the top and select 'Compress'.

steps.title: Locate the Compressed File
steps.detail: A new ZIP file will be created in the same location as the original files, named 'Archive.zip' or similar. You can rename it as needed.

faqs.question: Can I compress files into formats other than ZIP?
faqs.answer: Finder only creates ZIP files. For other formats, consider using third-party applications like Keka or WinZip.

faqs.question: Does compressing files reduce their quality?
faqs.answer: Compression reduces file size but does not affect the quality of files like images or audio. However, some formats may lose quality during compression.

faqs.question: Is there a limit to the size of files I can compress?
faqs.answer: There is no specific limit imposed by macOS, but very large files may take longer to compress and could affect system performance during the process.

caveats: Compression may not significantly reduce the size of already compressed files, such as JPEG images or MP3 audio files.
